'''Lloyd Hillyard Conover''' (June 13, 1923 – March 11, 2017) was an American chemist and the inventor of [[tetracycline]]. For this invention, he was inducted into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J15RAAAAMAAJ&q=lloyd%20conover|title=Inductees of the National Inventors Hall of Fame|date=1 January 2005|publisher=National Inventors Hall of Fame Foundation, Incorporated|via=Google Books}}</ref> Conover was the first to make an antibiotic by chemically modifying a naturally produced drug.<ref name=AMWS>"Lloyd Hillyard Conover." American Men & Women of Science: A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological, and Related Sciences. Detroit: Gale, 2008. Gale Biography In Context. Web. 19 Nov. 2011.</ref>  He had close to 300 patents to his name.

==Career==
In 1941, Conover began studying chemistry at [[Amherst College]], but his studies were interrupted by World War II. He then joined the Navy, serving three years in the Pacific on an amphibious [[Landing Ship, Tank|landing ship]],<ref name="LandingShip">{{cite web|last1=Theismann|first1=Jeanne|title=Visionary Veterans Exhibit in Alexandria|url=http://www.alexandriagazette.com/news/2016/nov/30/visionary-veterans-exhibit-alexandria/|website=Alexandria Gazette Packet|accessdate=13 March 2017|archive-date=13 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180713141449/http://www.alexandriagazette.com/news/2016/nov/30/visionary-veterans-exhibit-alexandria/|url-status=live}}</ref> ultimately rising to the rank of lieutenant junior grade. After the war, he returned to Amherst, receiving his B.A. degree in 1947.<ref name="NYT-obit" /> He went on to earn  his [[Ph.D.]] in chemistry from the [[University of Rochester]] in 1950.<ref name=AMWS/>

Upon completion of his studies, Conover joined [[Pfizer]]'s chemical research department. He was part of a team exploring the molecular architecture of the broad-spectrum antibiotics [[Terramycin]] and [[Aureomycin]].  Both of these drugs had been discovered as [[natural product]]s produced by [[actinomycetes]]. Working in conjunction with Harvard Professor R.B. Woodward, the team began to recognize that it was possible to chemically alter an antibiotic to produce other antibiotics that were effective in treating various types of illnesses. 
In 1952, he developed [[tetracycline]] in this way. Specifically, he was able to produce tetracycline by dechlorinating Aureomycin by catalytic reduction, that is, by substituting hydrogen for chlorine in chlortetracycline.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mIyxO5cLEAcC&q=lloyd%20conover&pg=PA5|title=Drug Discovery: Practices, Processes, and Perspectives|first1=Jie Jack|last1=Li|first2=E. J.|last2=Corey|date=3 April 2013|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9781118354469|via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Cb6BOkj9fK4C&q=lloyd%20conover&pg=PA305|title=Drug Discovery: A History|first=Walter|last=Sneader|date=23 June 2005|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9780471899792|via=Google Books}}</ref> His success led to the process being used to produce other superior structurally modified antibiotics. This is a standard practice in the industry today.

Conover applied for a patent on tetracycline in 1953,<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i4_FZHmzjzwC&q=lloyd%20conover%20patented%201955&pg=PA227|title=Antimicrobial Drugs: Chronicle of a Twentieth Century Medical Triumph|first=David|last=Greenwood|date=21 February 2008|publisher=OUP Oxford|isbn=9780199534845|via=Google Books}}</ref> and one was granted in 1955.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9HANBQAAQBAJ&q=lloyd%20conover&pg=PT42|title=God Is Here to Stay: Science, Evolution, and Belief in God|first1=Thomas R.|last1=McFaul|first2=Al|last2=Brunsting|date=8 April 2014|publisher=Wipf and Stock Publishers|isbn=9781630871802|via=Google Books}}</ref> Within three years, tetracycline became the most prescribed broad spectrum antibiotic in the U.S.  During this time, the patent was challenged.  In 1982, the courts upheld the patent and the right of scientists to patent based on similar methods.<ref>676 F.2d 51 216 U.S.P.Q. 1056, 1982-1 Trade Cases 64,578 In re COORDINATED PRETRIAL PROCEEDINGS IN ANTIBIOTIC ANTITRUST ACTIONS.Appeal of UNITED STATES of America.UNITED STATES of America, Appellant, v. PFIZER INC., American Cyanamid Company, Bristol-Myers Company, Olin Corporation, Squibb, Inc., E. R.Squibb & Sons, Inc., and The Upjohn Company. Nos. 81-1067, 81-1068.United States Court of Appeals, Third Circuit. Argued Feb. 1, 1982. Decided Feb. 16, 1982.  Retrieved June 8, 2011. http://bulk.resource.org/courts.gov/c/F2/676/676.F2d.51.81-1068.81-1067.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120524135951/http://bulk.resource.org/courts.gov/c/F2/676/676.F2d.51.81-1068.81-1067.html |date=2012-05-24 }}</ref>

In 1971, Conover became research director at [[Pfizer Central Research]] in [[Sandwich, England]]. In 1984, he retired as a senior vice president.

Conover died in [[St. Petersburg, Florida]], at the age of 93.<ref name="NYT-obit">{{cite news|last=Gellene|first=Denise|title=Lloyd Conover, Inventor of Groundbreaking Antibiotic, Dies at 93|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/12/business/lloyd-conover-dead-inventor-of-groundbreaking-antibiotic.html|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=March 12, 2017|archive-date=March 13, 2017|access-date=March 13, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170313112433/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/12/business/lloyd-conover-dead-inventor-of-groundbreaking-antibiotic.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
